Where it began

Isaac Vivian Alexander Richards was born in St John's, Antigua, on 7 March 1952. Cricket ran in the family: his brothers Mervyn and Donald both played for Antigua, and they pushed him to join in. He practised first with his father and a neighbour who had captained the island.

After school he worked at a bar and restaurant in St John's, and its owner kitted him out with whites, pads, gloves and a bat. In 1973 he went to England to play club cricket in Bath, where he also helped look after the ground. A contract with Somerset followed, and a flat in Taunton shared with a young Ian Botham.

The player

He made his Test debut against India in Bangalore in 1974 and hit an unbeaten 192 in only his second match. In 1976 he made 1,710 Test runs in the calendar year, a world record that stood for 30 years, and that summer he scored 291 at The Oval. In 121 Tests he made 8,540 runs at 50.24, with 24 hundreds and 45 fifties, and he held 119 catches.

He captained West Indies in 50 Tests, winning 27 and losing only eight, and never lost a series. In Antigua in 1986 he reached a hundred against England in 56 balls, at the time the fastest in Test history.

What made him special

He was the most commanding batter of his age. He hit good balls for four as a matter of routine, his favourite stroke whipping a good length from outside off stump through midwicket. He hooked fast bowlers without fear, and he never wore a helmet. Many of the great players who bowled at him, or simply watched him, rate him the best they saw.

His off-spin was a gentler business. His 32 Test wickets cost 61.38 each, which suggests his captains mostly wanted him for his batting and his fielding, and they were right.

Away from the middle

He won two World Cups with West Indies, in 1975 and 1979, with a hundred in the second final at Lord's. He won trophies with Somerset, and later with Glamorgan. His friendship with Ian Botham is one of the warmest in the game, and the trophy that replaced the Wisden Trophy for Tests between England and West Indies is named after the two of them, the Richards–Botham Trophy.

He was knighted in Antigua in 1999, and the Sir Vivian Richards Stadium carries his name. Wisden chose him as one of its five Cricketers of the Century. He has also been a summariser on the BBC's Test Match Special.

And finally

Even the masters have off days. In a World Cup match in 1983 he came back out after a break for bad light and took strike at the wrong end. It is one of the rarest sights in cricket, and it took a master to manage it.
